chooseSection.heading: How to Choose a Wealthfront Alternative
chooseSection.body:
Selecting a Wealthfront alternative starts with comparing percentage advisory fees against flat monthly charges. Wealthfront charges 0.25% per year, which amounts to $25 annually on a $10,000 balance. In contrast, flat fees take a fixed dollar amount regardless of portfolio growth: Acorns charges $4, $8, or $12 per month, while M1 charges a $3 monthly platform fee that is waived once platform assets exceed $10,000. On small accounts, a fixed $5 monthly fee equals $60 per year, which is 0.60% of a $10,000 account, whereas a percentage fee remains proportionate to the balance.

Account minimums also determine which services can be opened immediately. Wealthfront requires $1 to start a self-directed Brokerage Account, while Vanguard Digital Advisor requires $100 to enroll. Ally Invest Robo Portfolios also sets a $100 minimum. Fidelity Go requires $0 to open and $10 to begin investing. Schwab Intelligent Portfolios sets a higher entry threshold, requiring a $5,000 minimum balance to open an account.

Tax-loss harvesting rules vary widely across automated platforms. Wealthfront provides tax-loss harvesting across its taxable portfolios and publishes a claim that tax-loss harvesting can typically cover the annual fee more than 4.2 times over for Classic portfolio clients. Schwab Intelligent Portfolios offers tax-loss harvesting with no added advisory fee, but only for enrolled taxable accounts with at least $50,000. Fidelity Go reserves tax-loss harvesting for taxable accounts with $25,000 or more invested in stock-holding Flex Funds.

Cash management features differ in yield and structure. Wealthfront provides up to 4.45% APY through program banks with up to $8M in FDIC insurance eligibility. Betterment lists a Cash Reserve at a variable 3.50% base APY as of September 21, 2026, with an optional 0.75% boost for qualifying new clients up to $1M. M1 lists a High-Yield Cash Account at 3.35% APY with a $100 initial deposit. Ally Invest Robo Portfolios holds a 30% cash buffer earning 3.20% monthly interest in its cash-enhanced portfolio, though Ally notes that cash buffer is not FDIC insured.

Who this is not for: Investors who want an automated portfolio with no advisory fee may prefer zero-fee options. Wealthfront charges a 0.25% annual fee on automated portfolios, while services like Schwab Intelligent Portfolios charge no advisory fee. 

What would change the answer:
Several pricing moves could shift the comparative cost among Wealthfront alternatives. If Wealthfront adjusted its 0.25% advisory fee or altered its Cash Account APY structure, the cost gap against zero-fee options would shift. If Schwab Intelligent Portfolios lowered its $5,000 entry minimum or its $50,000 tax-loss harvesting requirement, it would become accessible to smaller taxable accounts. If Betterment removed its $5 monthly charge for accounts under $24,000 that lack recurring deposits, it would match Wealthfront at lower balances. If Fidelity Go changed its $25,000 threshold for free advisory services, smaller balances would face different fee calculations.

alternatives.heading: Betterment Pricing Among Wealthfront Alternatives
alternatives.body:
Betterment provides automated investing portfolios, tax-loss harvesting, a self-directed brokerage trading stocks and ETFs with no commission fees, and a Cash Reserve account. Betterment charges $5 per month for investing balances under $24,000, but reduces the fee to 0.25% annually if the client sets up monthly recurring deposits of $200 or more, or when the balance reaches $24,000. Balances between $1 million and $2 million pay a discounted 0.15% on that portion, and assets above $2 million pay 0.10%. Betterment also offers a Premium plan at a 0.65% annual fee that includes advisor access. Betterment waives wrap fees on self-directed assets.

Cash Reserve pays a variable base APY of 3.50% as of September 21, 2026, with a $10 minimum deposit, plus a 0.75% APY boost up to $1M for new clients through February 15, 2027, with up to $8M in joint FDIC insurance. Betterment checking has no foreign transaction or ATM withdrawal fees.

On a $10,000 balance without recurring deposits, Betterment costs $5 per month, totaling $60 per year. Wealthfront charges 0.25% on that same $10,000, which is $25 per year, making Wealthfront $35 cheaper. With $200 monthly recurring deposits, Betterment charges 0.25%, matching Wealthfront's $25 cost.

Betterment falls short of Wealthfront for investors with small balances who do not maintain a recurring deposit of $200, because the $5 monthly fee equals a higher percentage. Betterment fits investors who can deposit $200 each month or who hold more than $1 million to qualify for progressive tiered fee discounts.

alternatives.heading: Schwab Intelligent Portfolios Among Zero-Fee Wealthfront Alternatives
alternatives.body:
Schwab Intelligent Portfolios is an automated investment advisory service that charges no advisory fee and no commissions. Investors still pay the underlying operating expenses of the ETFs held in the portfolio. Schwab notes that it earns revenue from other sources, including Schwab ETFs management fees and cash allocation.

To open an account, Schwab Intelligent Portfolios requires a minimum investment of $5,000. Automated tax-loss harvesting is available at no extra fee, but clients must enroll and maintain at least $50,000 in a taxable portfolio.

On a $10,000 portfolio, Schwab Intelligent Portfolios charges $0 in advisory fees. Wealthfront charges 0.25%, which totals $25 per year. On a $50,000 portfolio, Schwab Intelligent Portfolios still charges $0 in advisory fees and activates tax-loss harvesting, whereas Wealthfront charges 0.25%, totaling $125 per year.

Schwab Intelligent Portfolios falls short of Wealthfront on account accessibility and lower-balance tax management. Wealthfront allows opening self-directed accounts with $1 and includes tax-loss harvesting on taxable portfolios without a $50,000 threshold. Schwab Intelligent Portfolios fits investors who have at least $5,000 to invest and want automated ETF management without paying an advisory fee.

alternatives.heading: Vanguard Digital Advisor Portfolios and Asset Costs
alternatives.body:
Vanguard Digital Advisor is an automated portfolio management service that builds portfolios using Vanguard ETFs. The service charges a $0 advisory fee for the first 90 days, though underlying ETF investment costs apply throughout. After the promotional period, Vanguard states an all-index portfolio costs about $15 to $16 per year for every $10,000 managed. For an active and index mix, the net advisory and fund cost is no more than $20 per $10,000 annually.

Vanguard Digital Advisor requires $100 in assets to enroll. Portfolio options include an all-index strategy, an active and index mix, and an environmental, social, and governance (ESG) allocation.

On a $10,000 balance in an all-index strategy, Vanguard Digital Advisor costs roughly $15 to $16 annually. Wealthfront's 0.25% advisory fee equals $25 per year before underlying ETF expenses. Over five years on a $10,000 balance, Vanguard's published all-index cost of $15 per year totals $75, while Wealthfront's advisory fee totals $125.

 Vanguard Digital Advisor fits investors who want low-cost index-based portfolio management from Vanguard with a low $100 entry requirement.

alternatives.heading: Fidelity Go Advisory Tiers and Coaching
alternatives.body:
Fidelity Go is an automated robo-advisor that scales advisory fees based on account size. Accounts with balances under $25,000 pay a $0 annual advisory fee. Accounts with $25,000 or more pay an annual advisory fee of 0.35%. There is no minimum balance required to open an account, though the balance must reach at least $10 before Fidelity Go invests the funds.

Clients with $25,000 or more receive unlimited one-on-one financial coaching sessions and automated tax-loss harvesting for taxable accounts invested in Fidelity Flex Funds that hold stocks. Fidelity Go provides financial planning tools to all customers regardless of balance.

On a $20,000 balance, Fidelity Go charges $0 in advisory fees. Wealthfront charges 0.25%, which totals $50 per year on $20,000. However, on a $30,000 balance, Fidelity Go's 0.35% fee equals $105 annually, whereas Wealthfront's 0.25% fee equals $75 annually, making Wealthfront $30 less expensive.

Fidelity Go falls short of Wealthfront on pricing once an account passes $25,000, charging 0.35% compared with Wealthfront's 0.25%. Fidelity Go fits investors with balances below $25,000 seeking free portfolio management, or those above $25,000 who want one-on-one financial coaching.

alternatives.heading: Ally Invest Robo Portfolios and Cash Buffers
alternatives.body:
Ally Invest Robo Portfolios offers two automated portfolio options with a $100 opening minimum. The cash-enhanced portfolio allocates roughly 30% of assets to an interest-earning cash buffer and charges no advisory fee. The market-focused portfolio keeps approximately 98% invested with roughly 2% cash and charges an annual advisory fee of 0.30%, which equates to $3 per $1,000 managed.

Both options provide fee-free portfolio rebalancing. The cash buffer earns 3.20% interest credited monthly, though Ally notes that the cash buffer inside the robo portfolio is not FDIC insured. For self-directed accounts, Ally offers a cash brokerage account with no minimum and a margin account with a $2,000 minimum. Ally also lists Personal Advice for accounts with at least $100,000.

On a $10,000 investment in Ally's market-focused portfolio, the 0.30% advisory fee equals $30 per year. Wealthfront's 0.25% fee equals $25 per year, saving $5 annually compared with Ally. In Ally's cash-enhanced portfolio, the advisory fee is $0, but $3,000 of a $10,000 balance remains uninvested in cash.

Ally Invest Robo Portfolios falls short of Wealthfront because its invested portfolio carries a higher 0.30% fee, and its cash-enhanced portfolio holds 30% out of the market without FDIC coverage. Ally Invest Robo Portfolios fits investors who want automated rebalancing with a built-in interest-bearing cash reserve.

alternatives.heading: Acorns Subscription Plans and Spare Change Roundups
alternatives.body:
Acorns operates on a tiered subscription pricing model rather than an asset-based percentage fee. The Bronze plan costs $4 per month, Silver costs $8 per month, and Gold costs $12 per month. Acorns also lists a Premium plan that includes a $10,000 life insurance policy and a will at no extra cost for eligible customers.

Core features include round-up investing of spare change. Silver and Gold tiers add the Acorns Later retirement account, offering a 1% match on new IRA contributions in the first year on Silver and a 3% match on Gold. Acorns provides an Emergency Savings account with a 3.59% variable APY as of September 22, 2026. Gold adds Early Invest, an investment account for children with a 1% match.

Acorns charges $48 annually on Bronze ($4 x 12), $96 annually on Silver ($8 x 12), and $144 annually on Gold ($12 x 12). On a $5,000 balance, Bronze at $48 per year represents an effective 0.96% fee, whereas Wealthfront's 0.25% fee equals $12.50. On a $50,000 balance, Acorns Bronze costs $48 per year (roughly 0.10%), while Wealthfront charges $125 per year.

 Acorns fits micro-investors who want automated spare-change roundups and retirement account matching incentives.

alternatives.heading: M1 Self-Directed Pies and Platform Fees
alternatives.body:
M1 charges no commission, trading, or management fees for its self-directed brokerage. It applies a $3 monthly platform fee, which is waived for clients who hold more than $10,000 in platform assets.

M1 provides a High-Yield Cash Account offering a 3.35% APY with a $100 initial deposit required to earn the stated yield. M1 also offers margin loans at 5.90% for accounts holding $2,000 or more in eligible securities. Account balances are protected by SIPC up to $500,000, which includes up to $250,000 for cash claims.

For an investor with an $8,000 balance, M1's $3 monthly fee totals $36 per year ($3 x 12), which represents an effective 0.45% fee. Wealthfront's 0.25% fee on $8,000 is $20 per year. Once an investor holds $12,000 on M1, the platform fee drops to $0, while Wealthfront charges $30 annually.

 M1 fits self-directed investors who hold more than $10,000 to avoid platform fees.

stillBetterFit.heading: When Wealthfront Is Still the Better Fit
stillBetterFit.body:
Wealthfront remains a practical option for investors who want completely automated portfolio management paired with integrated cash and borrowing features. Its 0.25% annual advisory fee covers personalized risk-adjusted portfolios, automatic rebalancing, and tax-loss harvesting for taxable accounts. Wealthfront publishes an example showing that a $15,000 balance incurs an estimated monthly cost of $3.18 at 0.25%, which totals $38.16 over twelve months (or $37.50 based on exact annualized math). Wealthfront also claims that its tax-loss harvesting typically covers the annual advisory fee more than 4.2 times over for Classic portfolio clients.

Beyond automated core portfolios, Wealthfront offers direct indexing and specialized products like a Bond Ladder. Its self-directed Brokerage Account allows clients to buy stocks and ETFs with a $1 starting minimum and zero advisory fees. For cash management, the Wealthfront Cash Account offers up to 4.45% APY (with a base APY of 3.55% as of November 13, 2026, plus an APY Boost up to a $150,000 balance) with zero account fees, free 24/7 instant withdrawals, and up to $8M in FDIC insurance eligibility through program banks.

Investors who want taxable accounts, retirement IRAs, and 529 college savings accounts in one system find Wealthfront well matched. While competitors charge flat monthly fees or require larger deposits for tax-loss harvesting, Wealthfront maintains uniform advisory pricing across its portfolio sizes.

verdict: Choosing among Wealthfront alternatives comes down to fee structures, minimum deposit requirements, and portfolio management preferences. Betterment and Fidelity Go offer percentage-based fees or fee waivers on specific balances, while Schwab Intelligent Portfolios and Vanguard Digital Advisor reduce or eliminate advisory fees for accounts meeting their entry thresholds. Acorns and M1 use flat subscription models that benefit specific balance tiers. Compare your current balance and required account features against published fees to find the right automated Wealthfront alternatives.

faqs.question: Which Wealthfront alternative has no advisory fee?
faqs.answer: Schwab Intelligent Portfolios charges a $0 advisory fee on portfolios with at least $5,000. Fidelity Go charges $0 in advisory fees on balances under $25,000. Ally Invest Robo Portfolios charges no advisory fee on its cash-enhanced portfolio with a 30% cash buffer. Vanguard Digital Advisor charges a $0 advisory fee for the first 90 days.

faqs.question: Do Wealthfront alternatives offer tax-loss harvesting?
faqs.answer: Yes, but requirements vary. Betterment features tax-loss harvesting on automated taxable accounts. Schwab Intelligent Portfolios offers tax-loss harvesting at no extra fee for enrolled taxable accounts of $50,000 or more. Fidelity Go provides tax-loss harvesting on taxable accounts with $25,000 or more holding stock Flex Funds.

faqs.question: What is the minimum deposit to open a Wealthfront alternative?
faqs.answer: Minimums range from $0 to $5,000. Fidelity Go requires $0 to open and $10 to invest. Betterment has no minimum balance. Vanguard Digital Advisor and Ally Invest Robo Portfolios require $100. M1 requires $100 for its High-Yield Cash Account stated APY, and Schwab Intelligent Portfolios requires $5,000.

faqs.question: Are advisory fees the only cost with robo-advisors?
faqs.answer: No, advisory fees do not cover ETF operating expenses. Investors across all platforms, including Wealthfront and its alternatives, pay the underlying expense ratios of the ETFs held in their portfolios. Some services also charge flat platform fees, such as M1's $3 monthly fee on balances under $10,000.

faqs.question: How do cash accounts differ between Wealthfront and its alternatives?
faqs.answer: Wealthfront offers up to 4.45% APY (base 3.55% as of November 13, 2026, plus APY Boost up to $150,000) with up to $8M FDIC insurance. Betterment Cash Reserve offers a variable 3.50% base APY as of September 21, 2026, plus a 0.75% boost up to $1M. M1 offers a High-Yield Cash Account at 3.35% APY, and Acorns offers Emergency Savings at 3.59% APY.
